470.title: Count the cost (Luke 14:25–33)
470.hook: a builder sits down to reckon before building a tower
470.howItsDone: Catholics preparing for baptism, marriage, ordination or religious vows go through a period of formation and discernment, so that, as Luke puts it, they sit down and count the cost before they promise.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a great supper, three thin excuses, and a house filled from the roadsides. Your line was compel them to come in. Which invitation did you accept? Day four hundred seventy, a new week.

Most towns have one: the half-built house. The foundation poured, the frame up, and then nothing. Weeds in the yard, plywood going gray, a for-sale sign that's been there three summers. Everyone who drives past knows the story without being told: somebody started and ran out of money. Jesus has great crowds walking with him on the road now. You'd think he'd be glad. Instead he turns around and says something that sounds almost designed to thin the crowd. Today, the half-built tower.
screen: `THE HALF-BUILT HOUSE IN TOWN.` → `SOMEBODY RAN OUT OF MONEY.` → `HE TURNS TO THE CROWD.`

segments.voice: First the hard sentence. If anyone comes to me and hates not his father and mother, and wife and children, and brothers and sisters, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple. It sounds shocking, and it's meant to stop you. But hate here is a Semitic way of speaking: to love one thing so much less than another that it looks like hate by comparison. Matthew's Gospel says it plainly: he that loves father or mother more than me. Jesus isn't canceling the commandment to honor your parents. He's asking what comes first. Then two pictures. "For which of you having a mind to build a tower, doth not first sit down, and reckon the charges that are necessary, whether he have wherewithal to finish it." Otherwise he lays the foundation, can't finish, and everyone laughs: this man began to build and was not able to finish. Second picture: a king with ten thousand soldiers hears another king is coming with twenty thousand. Doesn't he sit down first and think? If he can't win, he sends an embassy and asks for peace. Then the conclusion: every one of you that does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple. Notice what Jesus is not doing. He's not hiding the price to close the sale. Most recruiters do the opposite. He tells the crowd: sit down first. Count it. Know what this will ask of you before you start. And notice the word sit. Both the builder and the king sit down. Discernment, in Luke, is something you do slowly, in a chair, with the numbers in front of you.
screen: `HATE: LOVE LESS BY COMPARISON.` · `THE BUILDER SITS AND RECKONS.` · `THE KING WITH TEN THOUSAND.` · `NO HIDDEN PRICE.` · then, large: `SIT DOWN, AND RECKON THE CHARGES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: count the cost of one commitment. Settle, and breathe. Pick one thing you've said yes to, or are about to: a job, a relationship, a ministry, a habit, a promise. Sit with it the way the builder sits with his plans. What will it really take? Time, money, sleep, pride, other things you'll have to give up. Name the costs honestly, one at a time. Then ask: do I have enough to finish? If not, what would help? If you pray, ask for wisdom and for what you lack. The bell holds the time.
Count the cost. Jesus' warning to the crowds: sit down like a builder or a king and reckon what following him will take before you begin. Today's word.
Your line: sit down and reckon. Today, before you say yes to anything new, sit down for one minute and count what it will cost. Day four hundred seventy.

hate is a Semitic idiom for loving less; Matthew says loves father or mother more than me.
the builder and the king both sit down before acting
Luke uses the same picture for both: sit first, then decide.
Jesus hid the cost of discipleship to draw bigger crowds
he turned to the crowds and told them the cost up front.

fork.setup: you're a king with ten thousand soldiers. a king with twenty thousand is marching toward you. what do you do first?
options: march out at once.
sit down and consider whether you can win.
double your army by any means.
fork.reveal: Jesus says he sits down first, and if he can't win, sends an embassy while the other king is still far away and asks for peace.

trapdoor: what you thought: count the cost means Christianity is mostly about sacrifice.
what it means: Jesus asks people to know honestly what following him will ask before they begin, like a builder or a king.
what a scholar hears: the verb for reckoning, psephizo, comes from psephos, a pebble: counting with stones on a board.

471.title: The clever steward (Luke 16:1–13)
471.hook: a crooked manager is praised for being shrewd; you can't serve God and mammon
471.howItsDone: Catholics often speak of stewardship, the idea that time, talent and money are entrusted by God rather than owned outright, and many parishes ask members to make an annual stewardship commitment.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a builder sat down to count before he built his tower. Your line was sit down and reckon. What did you count? Day four hundred seventy-one.

Of all Jesus' parables, this is the one preachers tend to approach carefully. Readers have argued about it for many centuries, and commentators still disagree on parts of it. A manager is caught wasting his boss's money. He's about to be fired. So he spends his last afternoon cooking the books in his customers' favor. And at the end of the story, the boss praises him. It sounds like Jesus is applauding fraud. He isn't. But to see what he is doing, you have to watch the manager's hands. Today, the clever steward.
screen: `A PARABLE PREACHERS TIPTOE AROUND.` → `CAUGHT WASTING THE BOSS'S MONEY.` → `AND THE BOSS PRAISES HIM.`

segments.voice: A rich man hears his steward has wasted his goods. He calls him in: give an account, you're done. The steward thinks fast. I can't dig, I'm ashamed to beg. I know what I'll do, so that people will take me into their homes. He calls in his master's debtors one by one. How much do you owe? A hundred barrels of oil. Sit down quickly, write fifty. And you? A hundred measures of wheat. Write eighty. He's making friends with the only currency he has left. Then the surprising line: "And the lord commended the unjust steward, forasmuch as he had done wisely: for the children of this world are wiser in their generation than the children of light." Notice what's praised. Not the dishonesty. He's still called unjust. What's praised is that he saw the end coming and acted. He knew his position wouldn't last, and he used what was passing through his hands to make friends who would last. Jesus draws the lesson: make friends with the mammon of iniquity, so that when it fails, they may receive you into everlasting dwellings. Mammon is an Aramaic word for wealth, money and property, the things people trust in. Money will fail. Every one of us is a steward who will one day be asked to give an account. So use it now, while it's in your hands, for people. Then the line everyone remembers: "You cannot serve God and mammon." No servant can serve two masters. Money is a fine tool and a terrible boss. The steward was crooked, but he understood one thing perfectly: what you hold, you won't hold forever.
screen: `GIVE AN ACCOUNT. YOU'RE DONE.` · `A HUNDRED BARRELS? WRITE FIFTY.` · `PRAISED FOR SEEING THE END COMING.` · `MONEY WILL FAIL. FRIENDS REMAIN.` · then, large: `YOU CANNOT SERVE GOD AND MAMMON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: use money for friendship. Settle, and breathe. Picture what's passing through your hands this week: a paycheck, an allowance, a budget, even a few dollars. None of it stays. Now think of one person you could do something good for with a small part of it. Buy a coworker lunch. Pay for a friend's coffee. Send something to a family that's struggling. Pick one, and decide when. If you pray, ask to be a faithful steward. The bell holds the time.
The clever steward. A crooked manager praised not for cheating but for seeing the end coming and using money to make friends. Today's word.
Your line: god or mammon. Today, spend one small amount of money on purpose for someone else's good, and notice which master you're serving. Day four hundred seventy-one.

myth: Jesus praises the steward for cheating
he's still called unjust. he's praised for seeing the end coming and acting wisely.
the steward cut the debts to make friends who would take him in
he used what passed through his hands to make lasting friends.
mammon is the name of a demon in Luke's Gospel
it's an Aramaic word for wealth and property; later writers personified it.

fork.setup: you're the steward. you're fired, and you have one afternoon left with the books. what do you do?
options: beg the master for one more chance.
call in the debtors and cut their bills.
quietly take some money for yourself.
fork.reveal: he cuts their debts so they'll welcome him later. the master commends him for acting wisely, though he's still called unjust.

original.note: Greek, from Aramaic mamona: wealth, property, what a person trusts in.

trapdoor: what you thought: this parable says a little fraud is fine if it's clever.
what it means: the steward is still unjust; he's praised for seeing his time is short and using money to make lasting friends.
what a scholar hears: mammon comes from Aramaic, perhaps from a root meaning what is trusted; Luke calls the master kyrios, the same word used for Jesus, which is part of why readers argue.

472.title: Lazarus at the gate (Luke 16:19–31)
472.hook: a rich man never noticed the beggar at his own gate
472.howItsDone: Catholics hear the parable of the rich man and Lazarus at Sunday Mass in the year of Luke's Gospel, and popes, Paul VI and Francis among them, have used it to speak about the rich and the poor in today's world.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a crooked steward used his last afternoon to make friends with his master's money. Your line was god or mammon. Which master did you serve? Day four hundred seventy-two.

Outside almost every front door there's something nobody sees anymore. The recycling bin. The neighbor's car. Maybe a person sitting against the wall of the corner store you pass every day. Things right at your door can become invisible exactly because they're always there. Jesus tells a parable about two men separated by a single gate. One lives behind it in luxury. The other lies just outside it, every day. One of them has a name in the story. It's not the rich one. Today, Lazarus.
screen: `WHAT'S OUTSIDE YOUR FRONT DOOR?` → `ALWAYS THERE, SO INVISIBLE.` → `TWO MEN, ONE GATE.`

segments.voice: Luke paints the rich man in two strokes: clothed in purple and fine linen, feasting sumptuously every day. Purple dye was ruinously expensive, the color of kings. Then the other man: "And there was a certain beggar, named Lazarus, who lay at his gate, full of sores." He longs for the crumbs from the table, and the dogs come and lick his sores. Of all the people Jesus invents for his parables, Lazarus is the only one given a name. Abraham and Moses appear here too, but they come from Scripture. The rich man has no name. Later Latin readers called him Dives, but that's just the Latin word for rich. In the story, the beggar has a name, and the rich man has none. Both men die. Lazarus is carried by angels to Abraham's bosom. The rich man is in torment, and now he looks up and sees Lazarus. Notice: he knows his name. He knew it all along. He asks Abraham to send Lazarus with a drop of water, as if Lazarus were still a servant. Abraham answers gently, calling him son, and says a great chaos is now fixed between them. The rich man asks one more thing: send Lazarus to warn my five brothers. Abraham says: they have Moses and the prophets. Let them hear them. And the last line: if they won't hear Moses and the prophets, they won't believe even if someone rises from the dead. The rich man is never accused of hurting Lazarus. He's never cruel to him. His sin is simpler and more common: Lazarus was at his gate every day, and he stepped around him. The chasm after death is just the gate made permanent.
screen: `PURPLE AND FINE LINEN.` · `THE ONLY NAMED MAN JESUS INVENTS.` · `HE KNEW HIS NAME ALL ALONG.` · `THE GATE MADE PERMANENT.` · then, large: `A BEGGAR, NAMED LAZARUS, AT HIS GATE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice who is at your gate. Settle, and breathe. Walk in your mind along the route you take every day. Front door, street, store, office, school, the screen you scroll. Who's there, every day, that you've stopped seeing? Someone sitting outside. A lonely neighbor. A coworker who eats alone. A name you've never asked. Let one person come into focus. Picture learning their name today, or doing one thing for them. If you pray, pray for them by name if you know it. The bell holds the time.
Lazarus at the gate. The poor man with a name, lying every day at the door of a rich man who stepped around him. Today's word.
Your line: he was at the gate. Today, notice one person you usually walk past, and learn their name or meet their eyes. Day four hundred seventy-two.

he has no name. Dives is just the Latin word for rich.
Lazarus is the only character Jesus invents for a parable who gets a name
Abraham and Moses come from Scripture; of the people Jesus makes up, only the poor man has a name.
the rich man is accused of beating or robbing Lazarus
he's never cruel. he just stepped around him every day.

fork.setup: you're the rich man, in torment, and you can see Lazarus with Abraham. what do you ask for?
options: forgiveness from Lazarus.
send Lazarus with water, then to warn my brothers.
nothing; you accept it.
fork.reveal: he still treats Lazarus as a servant to be sent. Abraham says the brothers have Moses and the prophets.

original.note: Hebrew: Eleazar, God has helped. Lazarus is the Greek form of the name.

trapdoor: what you thought: the rich man went to torment for being rich.
what it means: he's condemned for not seeing the poor man at his own gate, every day, though he knew his name.
what a scholar hears: Lazarus, from Eleazar, means God has helped: the only invented parable character with a name, and it names the only help he got.

473.title: One came back (Luke 17:11–19)
473.hook: ten lepers healed, and one, a Samaritan, returns to say thank you
473.howItsDone: Catholics call the Mass the Eucharist, from the Greek for thanksgiving, and many make a short prayer of thanksgiving in silence after receiving Communion before leaving the church.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a rich man stepped around Lazarus every day. Your line was he was at the gate. Whose name did you learn? Day four hundred seventy-three.

When you were small, someone probably stood over you after a birthday with a pen and a stack of cards. Write your thank-you notes. It felt like a chore. But think about the last time someone came back, days later, just to say: what you did for me mattered. You probably remember it exactly. Jesus is still on the road to Jerusalem, passing along the border between Samaria and Galilee. At the edge of a village, ten men stand far off, because their disease means they have to keep their distance. Today, the ones who didn't come back, and the one who did.
screen: `WRITE YOUR THANK-YOU NOTES.` → `SOMEONE CAME BACK TO SAY IT.` → `TEN MEN STANDING FAR OFF.`

segments.voice: They lift up their voices: Jesus, master, have mercy on us. Leprosy in the Bible covers a range of skin diseases, and it meant exile. You lived outside the village, you called out a warning, you couldn't touch anyone. Jesus doesn't touch them this time. He just says: go, show yourselves to the priests. That's what the Law of Moses required when someone was healed, so the priest could declare them clean and they could go home. And as they went, they were cleansed. Walking down the road, not yet healed, then halfway there, healed. Nine keep walking. They're doing exactly what Jesus told them. "And one of them, when he saw that he was made clean, went back, with a loud voice glorifying God." He falls on his face at Jesus' feet, giving thanks. And Luke adds four words that land like a stone: and this was a Samaritan. The outsider. Then Jesus asks, almost to himself: "Were not ten made clean? and where are the nine?" He calls the man a stranger, a foreigner, the only one who came back to give glory to God. Then: arise, go thy way, thy faith hath made thee whole. Here's what a Catholic ear catches. Luke's Greek word for giving thanks is eucharistein. It's the root of Eucharist, the name Catholics give the Mass itself. The Samaritan, face down on the road, makes the first eucharist in this story: a healed man who turns around and gives thanks. The nine weren't bad. They were obedient. They were also in a hurry to get back to their lives. Only one stopped long enough to turn around.
screen: `TEN MEN STANDING FAR OFF.` · `HEALED WHILE WALKING.` · `ONE TURNS BACK: A SAMARITAN.` · `EUCHARISTEIN: TO GIVE THANKS.` · then, large: `WHERE ARE THE NINE?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank someone specifically. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the last month. Who helped you, and you kept walking? A doctor, a teacher, a friend who listened, a stranger who held a door at the right moment. Choose one. Now get specific: what exactly did they do, and what difference did it make? Plan how you'll tell them today, by message, call or in person, in words that name the thing. If you pray, give thanks to God for them too. The bell holds the time.
One came back. Of ten lepers healed on the road, only the Samaritan turned around to give thanks. Today's word.
Your line: where are the nine. Today, be the one who comes back: thank someone for one specific thing. Day four hundred seventy-three.

to the priests, as the Law required

as they went, they were cleansed: healed on the road.
the nine were disobeying Jesus
they were doing what he said: going to the priests. only one turned back.
the word Eucharist comes from the Greek for giving thanks

fork.setup: you're one of the ten. halfway to the priests, you look down and your skin is clean. what do you do?
options: keep going to the priests, as he said.
turn back to thank him.
run home to your family.
fork.reveal: nine keep going. one, a Samaritan, turns back, glorifying God with a loud voice, and falls at Jesus' feet.

original.note: Greek: giving thanks. The root of the word Eucharist.

trapdoor: what you thought: the nine were ungrateful people who disobeyed.
what it means: the nine obeyed and were healed. only the Samaritan stopped, turned back, and gave thanks and glory to God.
what a scholar hears: Luke uses eucharisteo, the verb behind Eucharist, and calls the man allogenes, a foreigner, a word found on the Temple's warning inscription.

474.title: The persistent widow (Luke 18:1–8)
474.hook: she wears down an unjust judge; pray always and don't lose heart
474.howItsDone: Catholics often pray for one intention over many days, as in a novena, nine days of prayer; Saint Monica, whose feast is August 27, is honored as a patron of those who pray for a long time for a loved one.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ten were healed and one came back. Your line was where are the nine. Who did you thank? Day four hundred seventy-four.

Picture a small-town courthouse with a judge everyone knows is on the take. He doesn't fear God, Jesus says, and he doesn't care what anyone thinks of him. No bribe, no hearing. And picture a widow with a case against someone who has wronged her. No husband to speak for her, no money to pay the judge, no lawyer. In that world she's about as powerless as a person can be. She has exactly one weapon. She keeps showing up. Luke tells us, before the story even starts, what it's for: that we ought always to pray, and not to faint. Today, the persistent widow.
screen: `A JUDGE WHO FEARS NO ONE.` → `A WIDOW WITH NO MONEY, NO HUSBAND.` → `ONE WEAPON: SHE KEEPS SHOWING UP.`

segments.voice: Here's the opening line in the Douay-Rheims: "And he spoke also a parable to them, that we ought always to pray, and not to faint." Faint, in old English, means lose heart, give up. The widow keeps coming to the judge: avenge me of my adversary. For a while he won't. Then he talks to himself, and it's almost funny. Although I don't fear God or respect anyone, yet because this widow is a bother to me, I'll give her justice, "lest continually coming she weary me." The Greek word behind weary me is a boxing term. It means to hit under the eye, to give someone a black eye. Some scholars think the judge is joking: if I don't rule for her, she'll come in here and punch me. Either way, the most powerless person in town wins by refusing to stop. Then Jesus draws the line. If an unjust judge gives in to persistence, how much more will God, who isn't unjust at all, do justice for his chosen who cry to him day and night? This is not a story that says God is like the judge. It's an argument from the lesser to the greater: God is the opposite of this judge. Then Jesus ends with a question that hangs in the air: when the Son of man comes, will he find faith on earth? Catholics remember Saint Monica here. For years she prayed for her son Augustine, who was living far from the faith. A bishop told her, as Augustine writes in his Confessions, that the son of so many tears could not be lost. Augustine became a bishop and a doctor of the Church.
screen: `ALWAYS TO PRAY, AND NOT TO FAINT.` · `LEST SHE GIVE ME A BLACK EYE.` · `GOD IS THE OPPOSITE OF THIS JUDGE.` · `MONICA'S YEARS OF TEARS.` · then, large: `PRAY ALWAYS. DON'T LOSE HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep praying for one thing. Settle, and breathe. Pick one request that matters to you and hasn't been answered: a person who's far away, an injustice that hasn't been fixed, a healing that hasn't come. Hold it up, the way the widow walked into the court one more time. Don't dress it up. Just bring it. If you pray, ask again, plainly. If you don't, simply hold the hope steady for a moment without letting it go. Decide to come back to it tomorrow. The bell holds the time.
The persistent widow. The powerless woman who wore down an unjust judge by never giving up, a parable about praying always and not losing heart. Today's word.
Your line: don't lose heart. Today, come back to your one request at least once more, at a set time, like showing up at court. Day four hundred seventy-four.

that we ought always to pray, and not to faint.
the Greek behind weary me can mean give me a black eye

fork.setup: you're a widow with no money and no one to speak for you. the judge has refused your case. what do you do?
options: give up; the system is rigged.
keep coming back until he rules.
find someone to bribe him.
fork.reveal: she keeps coming, and the judge gives in just to be rid of her. Jesus says: how much more will God do justice?

trapdoor: what you thought: if you nag God enough, God will finally give in.
what it means: if even an unjust judge yields to persistence, how much more will God, who is just, hear those who cry to him.
what a scholar hears: hypopiazo, to strike under the eye, is a boxing term Paul also uses (1 Corinthians 9:27); here the judge may be half joking.

475.title: The publican (Luke 18:9–14)
475.hook: O God, be merciful to me a sinner, and he went home justified
475.howItsDone: Many Catholics strike their breast at the words of the Confiteor at the start of Mass, and many pray the Jesus Prayer, built on the publican's words, slowly with the breath or on a prayer rope.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a widow wore down an unjust judge by never stopping. Your line was don't lose heart. Did you ask again? Day four hundred seventy-five.

Luke tells us who this story is for before he tells it: some people who trusted in themselves as just, and despised others. That's worth sitting with, because it's not a description of one group. It's a habit almost anyone can slip into. The scrolling that ends with at least I'm not like them. Two men go up to the Temple to pray at the same time. One is a Pharisee, careful and devout. The other is a publican, a tax collector working for Rome, a man his neighbors had reasons to resent. Today, two prayers.
screen: `WHO THE STORY IS FOR.` → `AT LEAST I'M NOT LIKE THEM.` → `TWO MEN GO UP TO PRAY.`

segments.voice: First the Pharisee. It's worth being fair to him, because the parable isn't a verdict on Pharisees as a whole. He's genuinely devout. He says: "O God, I give thee thanks that I am not as the rest of men", and then the list: not extortioners, unjust, adulterers, nor even like this publican. I fast twice in the week. I give tithes of all that I possess. Those are real practices, beyond what the Law required. The trouble isn't what he does. It's the comparison. He's praying with one eye on God and one eye on the man in the back. Now the publican. He stands far off. He won't even lift his eyes to heaven. He strikes his breast and says eight words: "O God, be merciful to me a sinner." No list. No comparison. No excuses. Just the truth and a request. And Jesus says: "this man went down into his house justified rather than the other." Justified means set right with God. Then the line we heard last week at the dinner table: everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and he that humbles himself shall be exalted. The publican's prayer has had a long life. Many Catholics strike their breast during the Confiteor at Mass, an echo of his gesture. And in the Eastern churches, the Jesus Prayer grew from his words and the blind man's cry: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner. The Catechism names it. It's one of the shortest prayers there is, and one of the most prayed.
screen: `I AM NOT AS THE REST OF MEN.` · `FASTING, TITHING, AND COMPARING.` · `HE STRIKES HIS BREAST.` · `HE WENT HOME JUSTIFIED.` · then, large: `O GOD, BE MERCIFUL TO ME A SINNER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray the publican's prayer. Settle, and breathe. Let your eyes lower, the way his did. Notice if your mind starts making a list, either of your good deeds or of other people's faults. Let the list go. If you pray, say his words slowly, in time with your breath: O God, breathing in; be merciful to me a sinner, breathing out. Repeat it, gently, as long as feels right. If you don't pray, simply sit with honesty about yourself, without comparing. The bell holds the time.
The publican. The tax collector at the back of the Temple who prayed eight words without comparing, and went home justified. Today's word.
Your line: be merciful to me. Today, when you catch yourself thinking at least I'm not like them, say the line instead. Day four hundred seventy-five.

O God, be merciful to me a sinner.

original.note: Greek: be merciful to me, from the word family of atonement and the mercy seat.

trapdoor: what you thought: Pharisees bad, tax collectors good.
what it means: a devout man who despises others and a sinner who simply asks for mercy; the second goes home set right with God.
what a scholar hears: hilaskomai belongs to the atonement word family; the Greek Old Testament calls the ark's cover the hilasterion, the mercy seat.

476.title: The pounds (Luke 19:11–27)
476.hook: servants given money to trade while the master is away
476.howItsDone: Catholics speak of the gifts given to every baptized person and of using them in service, and parishes often ask members to share their gifts, from music to accounting to visiting the sick.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a publican at the back of the Temple asked for mercy and went home justified. Your line was be merciful to me. Did you say it instead of comparing? Day four hundred seventy-six, the end of a week.

Jesus is nearly at Jerusalem now. He's just been to Jericho, where a short tax collector named Zacheus climbed a sycamore to see him. The crowd is buzzing. Luke says they thought the kingdom of God was about to appear immediately, any minute now, as soon as they reached the city. So Jesus tells them a story about waiting. A nobleman goes to a far country to receive a kingdom and come back. Before he leaves, he calls ten servants and hands each one the same small sum of money. Today, the pounds.
screen: `NEARLY AT JERUSALEM.` → `THE KINGDOM, ANY MINUTE NOW.` → `A STORY ABOUT WAITING.`

segments.voice: Each servant gets one pound. The Greek word is mina, a coin worth roughly a hundred days' wages by one common reckoning: real money, but not a fortune. And the instruction is two words in the Douay: "Trade till I come." Then the master's citizens send a message after him: we will not have this man to reign over us. Luke's first hearers may have caught an echo there. Some decades before, a son of Herod went to Rome to have his rule confirmed, and a delegation followed to oppose him. The master comes back a king anyway and calls in his servants. The first: your pound has gained ten pounds. "Well done, good servant, because thou hast been faithful in a little, thou shalt have power over ten cities." The second has made five, and gets five cities. Then a third comes with his pound wrapped in a napkin. I was afraid of you, he says, because you're an austere man. You take up what you didn't lay down. So I kept it safe. The master's answer is sharp: then why didn't you at least put it in the bank? The pound is taken from him and given to the one who has ten. Notice what the third servant got wrong. He didn't steal. He didn't waste. He just never used it, because he was afraid. Everyone started with the same pound. The difference was what they did with it while the master was away. Catholics read the pound as what everyone receives alike: faith, the word, the life of grace. Elsewhere Matthew tells a similar parable with talents, different amounts to each. Luke's version says: you all got the same gift. Trade with it.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: use one gift you've buried. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you're good at, or something you were given, that you've kept wrapped in a napkin. A voice you don't sing with anymore. A language you stopped speaking. A skill you're afraid to be seen trying. Patience, humor, a knack for fixing things. Pick one. Notice the fear that keeps it wrapped. Then picture unwrapping it once this week, for someone else. If you pray, thank God for the gift. The bell holds the time.
The pounds. Ten servants, one coin each, told to trade until the master returns; the one who buried his out of fear loses it. Today's word.

Your line: trade with it. Unwrap one buried gift this week. And that's week sixty-eight: count the cost, the clever steward, Lazarus, one came back, the persistent widow, the publican, and the pounds. Day four hundred seventy-six.

original.note: Greek: mina, a sum of money; the Douay translates it pound.

what it means: everyone receives the same gift; faithfulness means using it while the master is away, not burying it out of fear.
